paragraphs.heading: What coastal erosion is
paragraphs.text: Coastal erosion is a coastline losing ground: land is lost or shifted, and sediment and rock are carried off over long periods. The work is done by waves, currents, tides, water pushed by wind, ice floating in the water, and storms. As the shoreline moves inland, that retreat can be tracked over short repeating cycles such as tides and seasons. The forces behind it include hydraulic action, abrasion, and the wear of wind and water, some natural and some not.

paragraphs.heading: How waves break up a cliff
paragraphs.text: In hydraulic action, a wave striking a cliff squeezes the air trapped in its cracks. That squeezed air presses on the surrounding rock and, little by little, splits off fragments. Over time the cracks can widen, and sometimes they become a cave. Loose rock debris at the foot of a cliff, called scree, is thrown about too: the pieces knock into one another and become smaller, smoother and rounder, which is called attrition. When scree hits the base of the cliff it chips off more rock, working rather like sandpaper.

paragraphs.heading: Acids and sandblasting
paragraphs.text: Some rock is attacked chemically. Acids in sea water can dissolve rocks such as chalk and limestone, a process called solution or corrosion, and limestone cliffs are hit especially hard. Waves speed the reaction up by carrying away the material that has already reacted. Wind joins in where it blows strongly over loose sand and soft rock: millions of sharp grains blown against the rock act like a sandblaster, wearing, smoothing and polishing it.

paragraphs.heading: Why some coasts wear faster
paragraphs.text: How quickly a cliff retreats depends on many things. A rock's hardness is set by its strength and by any cracks, fractures or layers of loose material such as silt and fine sand. A beach in front of a cliff soaks up wave energy and shields the land behind it. The shape of the seafloor matters as well: shoals and bars offshore make storm waves break and lose their energy before they reach the shore.

paragraphs.heading: Hard rock and soft rock
paragraphs.text: Where a coast has rock layers or fracture zones of uneven strength, erosion picks out the difference. Soft patches wear away much faster than hard ones, which tends to leave tunnels, bridges, columns and pillars standing. Given enough time the coast tends to level out again. Sediment worn from the hard parts fills the soft ones, and the rock formations themselves are worn away.

paragraphs.heading: Rising seas and what people do
paragraphs.text: The IPCC expects sea level rise from climate change to step up coastal erosion around the world, greatly reshaping coasts and low-lying land. Erosion has already grown along the eastern seaboard of the United States and in parts of coastal Guyana. Florida and its counties have raised their budgets to replace lost sand, since beaches draw visitors and support tourism worth billions of dollars. People respond in three broad ways: soft controls, hard controls, or moving away. Hard structures such as seawalls and groynes last longer than soft measures, but they still wear out and must be repaired or rebuilt.
